lessons.title: Namespaces: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user with unshare
lessons.goal:
Create each kind of namespace by hand with `unshare` and see exactly what it isolates.

Why it matters: containers are not a kernel feature. They are ordinary processes placed in namespaces (what they can see) and cgroups (what they can use). Once you have done it by hand, Docker stops being magic.

setup.note: Most steps use `sudo unshare`; the user-namespace steps need no root. Nothing is installed or changed permanently. Never run `sudo unshare` demos on a machine you cannot afford to experiment on.

steps.title: A namespace is a private view
steps.text: A **namespace** wraps a global resource so that processes inside see their own copy. Linux has eight kinds: `mnt` (mount points), `pid` (process IDs), `net` (network stack), `uts` (hostname), `ipc` (message queues and shared memory), `user` (UIDs), `cgroup` and `time`. Every process belongs to one of each; `/proc/PID/ns/` links name them by inode number.

run.output: cgroup ipc mnt net pid pid_for_children time time_for_children user uts

steps.title: uts: a private hostname
steps.text: `unshare -u` starts a command in a new UTS namespace. Changing the hostname inside does not touch the host's.

run.cmd: h=$(hostname); sudo unshare -u sh -c 'hostname lab-container; echo "inside: $(hostname)"'; [ "$(hostname)" = "$h" ] && echo 'host hostname unchanged'

steps.title: The namespace is different from ours
steps.text: Comparing the link text of `/proc/PID/ns/uts` inside and outside shows two different namespaces.

run.cmd: a=$(readlink /proc/self/ns/uts); b=$(sudo unshare -u readlink /proc/self/ns/uts); [ "$a" != "$b" ] && echo 'different uts namespace inside'

steps.title: pid: the first process is PID 1
steps.text: In a new PID namespace the first process gets PID 1 and sees **only** processes in the namespace. `--fork` is needed because the process that calls `unshare` stays in the old namespace; `--mount-proc` mounts a fresh `/proc` for the new view.

run.cmd: sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc sh -c 'echo "my pid: $$"; ps -e -o pid,comm | cat'
run.output:
my pid: 1
    PID COMMAND
      1 sh
      2 ps
      3 cat

steps.after: Only the shell and `ps` exist. On the host the same shell has an ordinary large PID: the kernel gives each process one PID **per namespace level**.

steps.title: net: an empty network stack
steps.text: A new network namespace has only a down loopback interface: no addresses, no routes, no connectivity. That is why container networking needs `veth` pairs (module 28).

steps.title: mnt: private mounts
steps.text: Mounts made inside a mount namespace are invisible outside. We mount a tmpfs on `/mnt` inside and look from outside.

run.cmd: sudo unshare -m sh -c 'mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /mnt && echo inside > /mnt/f && echo "inside sees: $(ls /mnt)"'; echo "outside sees $(ls /mnt | wc -l) entries"
run.output:
inside sees: f
outside sees 0 entries

steps.title: user: root without privilege
steps.text: A **user namespace** maps IDs. `unshare -Ur` (no sudo!) creates one in which you are UID 0, mapped to your real UID outside. Inside you have a full set of capabilities **over the namespace's own resources**, but outside you are still an ordinary user. This is how rootless containers work.

run.cmd: touch mine; unshare -Ur ls -ln mine | awk '{print "inside the namespace the file owner is", $3}'; ls -ln mine | awk '{print "outside it is", $3}'
run.output:
inside the namespace the file owner is 0
outside it is 1000

steps.under: Namespaces are created by the `clone()` flags `CLONE_NEWNS`, `CLONE_NEWPID`, `CLONE_NEWNET`, `CLONE_NEWUTS`, `CLONE_NEWIPC`, `CLONE_NEWUSER`, or later with `unshare()`/`setns()`. A namespace lives as long as a process is in it or a file (bind mount or open descriptor) references it. Each kernel object (a socket, a mount, a process) stores a pointer to its namespace, so lookups use the caller's view.

options: Give processes a private view of a global resource
quiz.explain: They isolate what is visible; cgroups limit what is usable.

options: The calling process does not enter the new PID namespace; its child does
quiz.explain: Only children are created in the new PID namespace.

quiz.q: What does a new network namespace contain?

options: It creates a user namespace where you are root without real privileges

check.scenario: Explain in two sentences why a container is not a virtual machine.
check.answer: A container is an ordinary process (or tree of them) started in new namespaces and cgroups: it shares the **host's kernel**, so it starts in milliseconds and a kernel bug can affect all containers. A VM runs its own kernel on emulated or virtualised hardware, with a hypervisor between it and the host.

lessons.title: Entering namespaces: nsenter, ip netns, lifetime
lessons.goal:
Join a running namespace from outside with `nsenter`, see how named network namespaces are kept alive, and read the namespaces of any process.

Why it matters: `nsenter -t PID -n` is the standard way to debug a container's network from the host, and "where does this namespace live" explains leftovers after container crashes.

setup.note: Most steps use `sudo unshare`; the user-namespace steps need no root. Nothing is installed or changed permanently. Never run `sudo unshare` demos on a machine you cannot afford to experiment on.

steps.title: Start a process in new namespaces
steps.text: A background shell sleeps in its own network and UTS namespaces. We keep its PID.

run.cmd: sudo unshare -n -u sleep 300 & echo $! > pid.txt; sleep 0.5; p=$(pgrep -P $(cat pid.txt) sleep || cat pid.txt); echo $p > target.pid; ls /proc/$p/ns | wc -l | awk '{print $1, "namespace files for the target"}'
run.output:
[1] 409008
ls: cannot open directory '/proc/409013/ns': Permission denied
0 namespace files for the target

steps.title: Enter it with nsenter
steps.text: `nsenter -t PID -n COMMAND` runs a command inside the **network** namespace of process PID. Our tools stay the host's, only the namespace changes. `-u` for UTS, `-m` mount, `-p` pid, `-a` all.

run.cmd: sudo nsenter -t $(cat target.pid) -n ip -br link | awk '{print $1, $2}'
sudo nsenter -t $(cat target.pid) -u sh -c 'hostname lab-in-ns; hostname'

steps.title: Same process, two views
steps.text: From the host the process lives in a different network namespace than we do, which `ls -l /proc/PID/ns/net` shows by inode.

run.cmd: a=$(readlink /proc/self/ns/net); b=$(sudo readlink /proc/$(cat target.pid)/ns/net); [ "$a" != "$b" ] && echo 'target is in a different network namespace'
run.output: target is in a different network namespace

steps.title: Named namespaces: ip netns
steps.text: `ip netns add NAME` creates a namespace and **bind-mounts** its file onto `/run/netns/NAME`. That bind mount keeps the namespace alive even when no process runs in it. `ip netns exec` joins it by name.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns add lab-keep; ls /run/netns

steps.title: Lifetime and cleanup
steps.text: A namespace disappears when nothing references it. Delete the named one and stop the sleeper.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns del lab-keep; ls /run/netns 2>/dev/null | wc -l | awk '{print $1, "named namespaces left"}'
sudo kill $(cat pid.txt) 2>/dev/null; sleep 0.3; echo cleaned

steps.under: `lsns` lists the namespaces of all processes with the number of processes and the first one. A namespace with 0 processes can still exist (kept by a bind mount or an open file descriptor): leaked network namespaces after a crashed container runtime are found under `/run/netns` or `/var/run/docker/netns`.

options: Runs CMD inside the network namespace of PID
quiz.explain: It joins the namespace and runs the command.

quiz.q: How does `ip netns add` keep a namespace alive without processes?
options: A bind mount of the namespace file in /run/netns
quiz.explain: The bind mount holds a reference.

quiz.q: Which tool lists all namespaces on the host?

options: When no process or file reference remains

check.scenario: A container is stuck and you need to see its listening ports from the host without a shell in it. What do you run?
check.answer: Find its host PID (`docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' NAME`), then `sudo nsenter -t PID -n ss -ltnp` (and `ip addr`, `tcpdump -i eth0` the same way). The tools come from the host, so no shell or tools are needed in the container.

interview.a: mnt, pid, net, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time. See [the lesson](#/lesson/37/unshare-namespaces).

interview.q: What is the relationship between containers, namespaces and cgroups?
interview.a: A container is a process started in new namespaces (isolated view) and placed in cgroups (limited resources), with a root file system image. No separate kernel.

interview.q: How do you debug a container's network from the host?
interview.a: `nsenter -t PID -n ...` using the container's host PID. See [the lesson](#/lesson/37/nsenter-and-lifetime).

interview.q: What is a user namespace and why do rootless containers need it?
interview.a: It maps UIDs so a process is root inside with privileges only over the namespace's resources, while being an ordinary user outside. It lets unprivileged users create mount/pid/net namespaces.

interview.q: Why does the first process in a PID namespace matter?
interview.a: It is PID 1 there: it adopts orphans and must reap zombies, and if it exits the kernel kills every process in the namespace.

interview.q: What keeps a network namespace alive with no processes?
interview.a: A bind mount of its file (ip netns) or an open file descriptor to it.
